html:
A statement of faith issued in 638 by the emperor Heraclius, drafted by Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople. It declared that Christ had two natures but only one will. This view is called Monothelitism.

It was the last of many efforts to reunite the church after the Council of Chalcedon. Heraclius hoped that the formula of "one will" would satisfy Christians in Egypt and Syria who rejected Chalcedon's "two natures", while keeping the others on side. It was posted in the porch of Hagia Sophia.

It came too late and pleased no one. The Arab conquests were already taking Syria and Egypt, the very lands it was meant to hold. The popes in Rome condemned it, and the monk Maximus the Confessor fought it in writing. In 648 the emperor Constans II withdrew it and banned all debate on the subject. The Third Council of Constantinople condemned Monothelitism in 681.
